title: Is Ho Chi Minh City safe? Real risks and how to avoid them
description: Saigon safety for teachers: what the official advisories say, how phone snatching works, the scams, traffic rules and fines, and the emergency numbers to save.
h1: Is Ho Chi Minh City safe? The real risks for foreign teachers, and the habits that avoid them
intro: Ho Chi Minh City is generally safe for foreign teachers: the US rates Vietnam at its lowest travel-advisory level, 'exercise normal precautions', and the crime official advice warns about most is petty theft, above all bag-snatching by thieves on motorbikes. The risks you face every day are snatch theft and the traffic, both manageable with a few habits. In an emergency call 113 for police, 114 for fire and 115 for an ambulance.
keyPoints: **Official picture**: the US State Department keeps Vietnam at Level 1, 'exercise normal precautions' (June 2026); the UK warns that bag-snatching by thieves on motorcycles is common in crowded and tourist areas.

**Snatch theft** from passing motorbikes is the crime most likely to touch you: keep your phone away at the kerb and on the back of a Grab bike, carry bags on the side away from the road, and let go if someone grabs.

**Traffic** is the daily risk: the alcohol limit for riders is zero, a red light on a motorbike costs {{vnd:4000000-6000000}}, and US, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and Irish international driving permits are not valid in Vietnam.
**Emergency numbers**: 113 police, 114 fire and rescue, 115 ambulance, all free. 112 is for disasters and search-and-rescue, not Vietnam's 911.
**Legal traps** catch newcomers: vaping is banned ({{vnd:3000000-5000000}} fine), police drug-test at nightlife venues and private parties, and changing money at gold shops is an offence.
**Health**: the city had recorded 24,651 dengue cases in 2026 by 2 August; for a fever, take paracetamol only and get tested.

sections.title: How safe is Ho Chi Minh City, really?

blocks.text: Governments that track crime against their citizens abroad agree on the shape of the risk. The [US State Department](https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/vietnam.html) rates Vietnam Level 1, 'exercise normal precautions' (issued 24 June 2026), and notes that petty crime is common in busy tourist areas. The [UK travel advice](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/vietnam/safety-and-security) says bag-snatching by thieves on motorcycles is common in crowded and tourist areas, and that petty crime rises around Christmas and Tet.

Two ratings look worse and need reading carefully. OSAC, the US State Department's security advisory council, rates both Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City as [high-threat locations for crime](https://osac.gov/Content/Report/182396b7-4bda-40e2-98c5-1c4093caea15) affecting US government interests. And on [Numbeo's 2026 mid-year quality-of-life data](https://www.numbeo.com/quality-of-life/rankings.jsp?title=2026-mid), contributors rate Saigon's safety at 50.2 against Hanoi's 66.2. Numbeo's score is a perception survey, not crime statistics, but it matches what the advisories describe: a big, busy city where theft is the problem you are most likely to meet.

sections.title: Phone and bag snatching: how it happens and how to avoid it

blocks.text: The classic theft in Saigon is fast and from a moving motorbike: a phone lifted out of your hand at the roadside, or a bag pulled off your shoulder from the traffic side. The [UK advice](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/vietnam/safety-and-security) is to carry bags on the side away from traffic and to **hand over valuables rather than resist**. A phone can be replaced; don't get pulled towards the traffic over one.

items: Don't use your phone at the kerb. Step into a doorway or a shop to check a map or book a ride.
Don't film traffic or the street on the busiest strips, such as Nguyen Hue and Bui Vien, with your phone held out towards the road.
Put your phone away while riding pillion on a Grab or Xanh SM bike; a phone held up for navigation is an easy grab.
Carry a zipped cross-body bag in front of you or on the side away from the road, and don't hang a bag from the handlebars or footwell of a bike.
Be extra careful around Christmas and Tet, when the UK advice says petty crime rises.
Never leave your passport as a deposit with a landlord or a bike-rental shop; the UK advice warns against it.

blocks.text: If your phone or bag is snatched

items.title: Let go and get safe
items.text: Don't chase the bike. If you are hurt or threatened, call 115 for an ambulance or 113 for the police.

items.title: Lock the phone and protect your money
items.text: From another device, lock or erase the phone, change your email and banking passwords, and call your bank to block your cards.

items.title: Sort out your number at a carrier store
items.text: Take your passport to your carrier's store. Since [15 June 2026](https://luatvietnam.vn/dan-su/thong-tu-08-2026-tt-bkhcn-huong-dan-xac-thuc-thong-tin-thue-bao-di-dong-mat-dat-430575-d1.html), putting your SIM in a new phone blocks outgoing calls and texts within 2 hours until you redo the face check, and you have 30 days before the number is cut off both ways. Our [SIM and eSIM guide](/esim-vietnam-guide) covers numbers and carriers.

items.title: Get a report if your insurer needs one
items.text: If you will claim on travel or contents insurance, ask the insurer what proof it accepts first. A colleague or your school's office staff can help you explain what happened to the local police in Vietnamese.

sections.title: Common scams and traps for new arrivals

blocks.text: Most scams aimed at foreigners in Saigon are small and avoidable. The one that can wreck your year is a fake job offer, which is why it has [its own guide](/teach-in-vietnam/teaching-job-scams-in-vietnam). The rest are about transport, drinks, money and documents.

blocks.caption: Scams and traps that catch newcomers in Ho Chi Minh City, and the defence (UK travel advice, Vietnamese law and employers' own warnings)
rows: Fake or too-good job offers

An offer that looks too good to be true; the [UK advice](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/vietnam/safety-and-security) says such offers have ended in people being trafficked to neighbouring countries to work in online scams
Never pay to get a job; check the employer and the contract before you travel or move
Fake recruiters using real school names
Pages copy a known school's logo and ask for money, ID photos or an app download
[VUS](https://teachenglish.vus.edu.vn/fake-job-warning) says applying is free and any request for money is a scam
Unofficial taxis and transfers
Unmetered cars, and free airport bus transfers you did not arrange
Book Grab, Xanh SM or Be in the app, or use a metered taxi
Drink spiking and methanol
Spiked drinks, and cheap spirits cut with methanol, which has killed people even in licensed venues
Keep your drink in sight; prefer sealed bottles and known brands
Passport as a deposit
A landlord or bike-rental shop asks to keep your passport
Refuse; you need it for your SIM, bank and work paperwork
Street money changers and gold shops
A better rate for your dollars, outside a bank
It is an offence for you, not just them; change money only at banks or licensed counters

blocks.text: On the last point: under [Decree 340/2025/ND-CP](https://baovanhoa.vn/phap-luat/phat-toi-100-trieu-dong-neu-mua-ban-ngoai-te-tai-to-chuc-khong-duoc-phep-thu-doi-ngoai-te-193545.html), in force since 9 February 2026, the person changing money at an unlicensed place is penalised, not only the shop. Below US$1,000, a first offence gets a warning. Larger amounts, or a repeat offence, are fined from {{vnd:10000000-20000000}} upwards, and the cash can be confiscated. Where to change money safely, and what ATMs charge foreign cards, is in [banking and sending money home](/teach-in-vietnam/banking-and-sending-money-home-from-vietnam#cash-and-atms).

For housing, use the eno.vn guides to [renting an apartment](/renting-an-apartment-vietnam-foreigner) and [getting your deposit back](/rental-deposit-vietnam); for a bike, the [motorbike rental guide](/motorbike-rental-ho-chi-minh-city).

sections.title: Traffic safety: the risk you face every day

blocks.text: Many teachers get around by motorbike, their own or a Grab bike. The [Road Traffic Order and Safety Law](https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2026/3/55-vbhn-vpqh.pdf) (in force since 1 January 2025) bans riding without a valid licence, riding with **any** alcohol in your blood or breath, and holding or using a phone while riding. Passengers must wear a helmet too; Grab drivers carry one for you.

Under [Decree 168/2024/ND-CP](https://luatvietnam.vn/giao-thong/nghi-dinh-168-doi-voi-xe-may-863-100609-article.html) a red light costs {{vnd:4000000-6000000}}, any alcohol at all from {{vnd:2000000-3000000}}, no helmet or an unfastened one {{vnd:400000-600000}} and riding a bike up to 125 cc without a valid licence {{vnd:2000000-4000000}}, and camera-based fines sent later are widely used; the full table is in [motorbike licences for foreigners](/teach-in-vietnam/motorbike-licence-in-vietnam-for-foreigners#traffic-fines-decree-168). The bigger cost of riding illegally is the crash, not the fine: compulsory third-party insurance ({{vnd:60000}} a year) [pays other people](https://vietnamfinance.vn/boi-thuong-toi-da-150-trieu-dongnguoi-trong-mot-vu-tai-nan-d100407.html), not your own hospital bill, and travel or health insurers may refuse a motorbike claim if you had no locally valid licence.

blocks.title: Your international driving permit may be worthless here
blocks.text: Vietnam recognises an international driving permit only if it was issued by a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention, and only together with your valid home licence. On the [UN treaty record](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XI-B-19&chapter=11&Temp=mtdsg3&clang=_en), the UK, South Africa and the Philippines are parties; the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, India and Japan are not, so permits from those countries give you no legal cover on a Vietnamese road. See [motorbike licences for foreigners](/teach-in-vietnam/motorbike-licence-in-vietnam-for-foreigners) for the legal routes, and use Grab, Xanh SM or Be until you have one.

items: **Ride defensively**: expect bikes from every direction, including the wrong way and on the pavement, and look before you step off the kerb.
**Crossing on foot**: walk at a steady, predictable pace so riders can steer around you; don't stop or run.
**Rain**: storms are usually short afternoon or evening bursts. Don't ride through deep floodwater, where engines stall and drains are open; wait it out.

**The one exception to the licence rule**: a moped with a design speed of up to 50 km/h and an engine of up to 50 cc (or an electric motor up to 4 kW) needs no licence for anyone aged 16 or over, though registration and insurance are still required. Most scooters exceed these limits.

blocks.text: For routes, the metro and ride-hailing apps, see [getting around Ho Chi Minh City](/teach-in-vietnam/getting-around-ho-chi-minh-city).

sections.title: Health risks that catch newcomers out

blocks.text: The health risks are mostly about mosquitoes, animals and what you drink. The [US CDC](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/destinations/traveler/none/vietnam) keeps Vietnam at Level 1, recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid vaccines plus routine ones, advises Japanese encephalitis vaccination for anyone moving there, and reports no malaria transmission in Ho Chi Minh City.

items: **Dengue**: the city recorded [24,651 cases](https://vov.vn/xa-hoi/ca-sot-xuat-huyet-o-tphcm-tang-20-benh-nhan-can-chu-y-giai-doan-nguy-hiem-post1320192.vov) in 2026 up to 2 August, in all 168 wards and communes. Use repellent at dawn and dusk in the rainy season. For a fever, take paracetamol only (no ibuprofen or aspirin), get tested, and get care for lethargy, abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or bleeding; days 3–7 are the dangerous phase.

**Rabies**: southern provinces recorded [nearly 20 rabies deaths](https://vnexpress.net/vi-sao-so-ca-dai-tang-5092402.html) in the first half of 2026. After any dog or cat bite, wash the wound with soap under running water for at least 15 minutes and get assessed for vaccine the same day.

**Methanol**: the [UK advice](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/vietnam/safety-and-security) reports methanol poisoning from licensed bars, shops and hotels. Avoid cheap spirits of unknown origin.
**Water and air**: drink bottled or filtered water, or boil tap water. In the dry season (December to April), check the air-quality index and wear a well-fitting mask on hazy days when riding.

sections.title: Laws that get foreigners into trouble

blocks.text: For many teachers the real danger is not crime but breaking a rule they did not know about. These rules apply to foreigners in full.

blocks.text: Nitrous-oxide balloons are widely sold in nightlife areas, the UK advice notes; skip them. On the work permit, only teach once yours is issued, and let your employer handle the filing; [the work permit guide](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnam-work-permit-for-english-teachers) explains how it works.

sections.title: Emergency numbers and who to call

blocks.text: Vietnam has separate free numbers for police, fire and ambulance; Ho Chi Minh City [linked its 113, 114 and 115 lines into one system](https://vov.vn/xa-hoi/tphcm-ra-mat-he-thong-tong-dai-khan-cap-lien-thong-113-114-115-782233.vov) in 2015. English support is limited, so for a medical emergency the private hospitals' own emergency lines are an alternative. Save these before you need them.

blocks.text: Hospital addresses come from the [Australian Government's July 2026 list](https://hcmc.vietnam.embassy.gov.au/files/hchi/list_of_hospitals_jul_2026.pdf), which uses the new ward names: since 1 July 2025 the city has no districts officially, so 'District 7' or 'Thao Dien' are informal names. Give a driver or dispatcher both the old and the new name.

blocks.text: Setting all of this up in your first fortnight — SIM, bank, clinic, transport — is covered step by step in [your first weeks in Ho Chi Minh City](/teach-in-vietnam/your-first-weeks-in-ho-chi-minh-city).

faqs.q: Is Ho Chi Minh City safe for a woman moving alone?
faqs.a: The risks described in official advice, mainly snatch theft, drink spiking and traffic, apply to everyone, and the same habits cover them: app-booked rides at night, your drink in sight, and your phone away at the roadside. Check your own government's travel advice before you go, and ask other teachers at your school which streets they avoid.

The main risks after dark are the same as by day, plus drink spiking, methanol in cheap spirits and police drug raids at nightlife venues. Book a ride in the Grab, Xanh SM or Be app to get home rather than walking long distances or hailing an unmetered car.

faqs.q: Is Ho Chi Minh City safer than Hanoi?
faqs.a: On Numbeo's 2026 mid-year data, contributors rate Hanoi safer (66.2 against 50.2), but that is a perception survey, not crime statistics. Official advisories cover Vietnam as a whole, and both cities share the same main risks: snatch theft and traffic.

faqs.q: Is 112 the emergency number in Vietnam?
faqs.a: No. Call 113 for police, 114 for fire and rescue, and 115 for an ambulance. Since September 2025, 112 has been a national line for disasters, incidents and search-and-rescue, linked to the other three but not a replacement for them.

faqs.q: Is the tap water safe to drink in Saigon?
faqs.a: Don't drink it straight from the tap. Drink bottled or filtered water, or boil tap water first.
They are the normal way to get around, and the driver carries a helmet for you, which you must wear by law. Keep your phone in your pocket during the ride and hold your bag in front of you.
